care_notes: A single male needs a heated, filtered, lidded tank with a footprint of at least 45x30 cm; bettas breathe air at the surface, so surface area matters more than depth. They need a heater — Seriously Fish gives 22-30 C and Aquarium Co-Op targets around 27 C, and unheated rooms below 22 C cause lethargy and infection. Feed a betta-specific pellet once daily, only as much as it eats in about a minute. Never house two males together, and add tank mates only in tanks of 38 L or more with heavy planting and escape routes.
common_mistakes: Keeping them in unheated, unfiltered bowls or vases
Assuming the labyrinth organ means they do not need clean water or filtration
Overfeeding, which causes bloating and constipation
Housing with fin-nippers or with other long-finned, brightly coloured fish
Putting two males, or a male and female outside breeding, in one tank
disputed: Minimum volume is commonly cited between 19 L and 40 L. Aquarium Co-Op accepts 5 gal (19 L) as workable and prefers 10 gal (38 L); Seriously Fish specifies a 45x30 cm base, which is about 38-40 L at normal tank heights. We list the larger figure. Temperature also disputed: Seriously Fish gives a wide 22-30 C tolerance, Aquarium Co-Op recommends around 27 C.
description: The Siamese fighting fish, commonly known as the Siamese fighter, or locally as the betta, is a freshwater fish native to Mainland Southeast Asia, namely Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam. It is one of more than 70 species of the genus Betta, but the only one eponymously called "betta", owing to its global popularity as a pet; Betta splendens are among the most popular aquarium fish in the world, due to their diverse and colorful morphology and relatively low maintenance.
native_range: Mainland Southeast Asia, namely Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam

care_notes: Guppies are hard-water fish: they want pH above 7.0 and plenty of calcium and magnesium, and they do badly in soft, acidic, RO-based water. Keep two to three females per male, or a single-sex group, otherwise females are harassed constantly. They breed roughly every 30 days and a tank fills fast, so plan for fry or plan to rehome them. Cooler water around 22-24 C extends lifespan; keeping them at 28 C speeds growth but shortens life to about 18 months.
common_mistakes: Keeping more males than females, so females are chased to exhaustion
Soft or RO water without remineralising, causing wasting and fin problems
Not planning for fry, leading to a badly overstocked tank within months
Housing with fin-nippers such as tiger barbs or serpae tetras
Buying heavily inbred fancy strains and expecting them to be as hardy as older stock
disputed: Aquarium Co-Op allows a trio in a 5 gal (19 L) tank but recommends 38-76 L long term; Seriously Fish specifies 45x30x30 cm (about 40 L). We list 40 L. Temperature ranges also differ: Seriously Fish gives 17-28 C tolerance, Aquarium Co-Op recommends 24-26 C.
description: The guppy, also known as the millionfish or rainbow fish, is a member of the family Poeciliidae and, akin to most New World members of the family, is classified as a livebearer. Male guppies, which are smaller than females, have ornamental caudal and dorsal fins. Wild guppies generally feed on a variety of food sources, including benthic algae and the larvae of aquatic insects.
native_range: northeast South America, it has been introduced to many environments and are now found all

care_notes: Endlers are smaller and generally hardier than fancy guppies, and tolerate a very wide range of hardness and temperature, including unheated rooms in warm climates. They hybridise freely with guppies and produce fertile offspring, so never mix the two if you care about keeping a pure line. Broods of 5-25 arrive every 23-30 days, so a colony grows quickly. Because of their small size they are best in a species tank or with other nano fish, not a general community.
common_mistakes: Keeping them with guppies, which produces hybrids and destroys both lines
Housing them with fish large enough to eat them
Not accounting for exponential colony growth in a small tank
Assuming they need heated tropical temperatures everywhere - in most of India they need no heater
disputed: Aquarium Co-Op gives a 5-10 gal (19-38 L) minimum and says room temperature is fine; Seriously Fish specifies 45x30x30 cm (about 40 L) and a warmer 24-30 C. We list 38 L and a range spanning both temperature positions.
description: Poecilia wingei, known to aquarists as Endlers or Endler's livebearer, in the genus Poecilia, is a small fish native to the Paria Peninsula in Venezuela. They are prolific breeders and often hybridize with guppies. These very colorful hybrids are the easiest to find being offered in pet-shops, typically under the name Endler's guppy.
native_range: the Paria Peninsula in Venezuela

images.attribution: (c) Aiman Azmi, some rights reserved (CC BY-NC-SA)

care_notes: Platies are one of the genuinely easy beginner fish: peaceful, hard-water tolerant, and happy anywhere from 20-28 C. Keep at least two females per male or the females are harassed. They produce 20-50 fry a month once mature, and will also hybridise with swordtails if both are present. They need vegetable matter in the diet, not just protein flake.
common_mistakes: Buying only males and females at random rather than a 1:2 or 1:3 ratio
Ignoring the breeding rate until the tank is overstocked
Keeping them in soft water without mineral supplementation
Uncovered filter intakes that suck in fry
disputed: Aquarium Co-Op suggests 10-20 gal (38-76 L); Seriously Fish specifies 60x30x30 cm (about 54 L). We list 54 L as the floor.
description: The southern platyfish, common platy, or moonfish is a species of freshwater fish in family Poeciliidae of order Cyprinodontiformes. A live-bearer, it is closely related to the green swordtail and can interbreed with it. It is native to an area of North and Central America stretching from Veracruz, Mexico, to northern Belize.
native_range: an area of North and Central America stretching from Veracruz, Mexico, to northern Belize

care_notes: Mollies are the largest of the common livebearers - females reach 12 cm - and they are hard-water fish that fail in soft, acidic tanks. Most stock is farmed in brackish or heavily mineralised water, and moving them into soft tap water stresses the kidneys and triggers ich, fungus and 'shimmying'. Add crushed coral or a mineral supplement if your GH is below 10. They need a genuine vegetable component in the diet, and a 90 cm tank because they are large, active grazers.
common_mistakes: Keeping them in soft water, the single biggest cause of molly deaths
Adding aquarium salt as a substitute for actual hardness and minerals
Underestimating adult size and buying a 40 L tank for them
Feeding only protein flake with no vegetable matter
Mixing balloon-body strains with normal ones and expecting the same lifespan
disputed: Minimum volume is commonly cited between 76 L and 208 L. Seriously Fish specifies 90x30x30 cm (about 81 L) for the short-finned molly; Aquarium Co-Op says 20 gal (76 L) minimum but 29-55 gal (110-208 L) for larger sailfin types. We list 80 L for P. sphenops and flag that sailfin mollies need substantially more. Some published guides listing 40 gal (151 L) as the minimum for all mollies are conflating sailfin and short-finned types.
description: Poecilia sphenops, called the Mexican molly or simply the molly, is a species of poeciliid fish from Central America. It was once understood as a widespread species with numerous local variants ranging from Mexico to Venezuela, but these variants are today considered distinct species belonging to the P. sphenops complex and P. sphenops itself as being native to Mexico, Guatemala, and Honduras. Due in part to its popularity as an aquarium fish, the species has been introduced outside of its native range, but many records may in fact refer to P. mexicana or other species from the complex. P. sphenops has been crossbred with other mollies, notably P. latipinna and P. velifera, to produce fancy mollies for the ornamental fish trade.
native_range: Mexico, Guatemala, and Honduras

images.attribution: (c) Daniel Pineda Vera, some rights reserved (CC BY)

care_notes: Swordtails are much bigger than shops imply - females reach 16 cm total length - and they are strong, restless swimmers that need tank length rather than volume. Males form dominance hierarchies and a subordinate male in a short tank gets chased relentlessly, so keep one male with several females or an all-female group. They are hard-water fish like platies and hybridise with them readily. They are accomplished jumpers, so a tight lid is essential.
common_mistakes: Buying them for a 60 cm tank based on the 5 cm juvenile size in the shop
Keeping two or more males in a tank too short for one to escape the other
No lid - swordtails jump out routinely
Soft water, which they tolerate poorly
disputed: This is the largest disagreement in the livebearer set. Seriously Fish specifies a 120x30 cm base (about 108-126 L); most hobby guides and retailers say 20-29 gal (76-110 L). We list 110 L with a 120 cm length requirement, siding with the larger figure because these are fast, long-bodied swimmers.
description: The green swordtail is a species of freshwater/brackish fish in family Poeciliidae of order Cyprinodontiformes. A live-bearer, it is closely related to the southern platyfish or 'platy' (X. maculatus) and can crossbreed with it. It is native to an area of North and Central America stretching from Veracruz, Mexico, to northwestern Honduras.
native_range: an area of North and Central America stretching from Veracruz, Mexico, to northwestern Hon

images.attribution: (c) Kaden Slone, some rights reserved (CC BY)

care_notes: Fancy goldfish are coldwater fish that reach 15-20 cm and live for decades, and they produce far more waste than any tropical fish of the same length. Aquarium Co-Op's rule of 20 gal (76 L) for the first fish plus 10 gal (38 L) for each additional one is the most defensible figure; Practical Fishkeeping's rule of six times adult length by twice adult width gives a similar 90x35 cm footprint. They need no heater in most homes, but they suffer above about 24 C, which matters in much of India - a chiller, a cool room, or simply not keeping goldfish is the honest answer in a 32 C flat. Wide, shallow tanks beat tall ones because oxygen exchange and swimming room both scale with surface area.
common_mistakes: Bowls and 20-40 L 'goldfish tanks', which are the classic beginner killer
Assuming a 3 cm shop fish stays small - they reach 15-20 cm
Adding a heater and keeping them at tropical temperatures
Keeping fancy varieties in strong flow, which they cannot swim against
Housing fancies with fast single-tailed goldfish or comets that outcompete them at feeding
disputed: Minimum volume is commonly cited between 57 L and 150 L for a single fancy goldfish. Aquarium Co-Op says 20 gal (76 L) per fish plus 10 gal (38 L) each additional; Practical Fishkeeping recommends a 60 cm tank as an absolute floor but a 90x30 cm tank for adults. Published figures of 57 L (15 gal) are below every reputable source we checked and should not be used. Temperature is also disputed: Aquarium Co-Op gives 10-21 C, other sources allow up to 24 C.
description: The goldfish is a freshwater fish in the family Cyprinidae of the order Cypriniformes. It is commonly kept as a pet in indoor aquariums, and is one of the most popular aquarium fish. Goldfish released into the wild have become an invasive pest in parts of North America and Australia.
native_range: China, the goldfish is a relatively small member of the genus Carassius (which also includ

care_notes: Zebra danios are hardy but they are not nano fish: Seriously Fish specifies a 90x30 cm base because they are relentless, fast swimmers that cover the whole tank all day. They are subtropical, doing best at 18-25 C, and are frequently kept too warm alongside tropical community fish. Keep 8 or more - small groups become nippy and stressed. They jump, so keep a tight lid.
common_mistakes: Selling them as a 20-40 L 'starter tank' fish when they need 90 cm of swimming length
Keeping fewer than 6-8, which turns them into fin-nippers
Keeping them at 26-28 C with tropical fish when they prefer 18-25 C
Housing them with slow or long-finned fish such as bettas and angelfish
Using them to cycle a new tank ('fish-in cycling')
disputed: Minimum volume is commonly cited between 38 L and 81 L. Aquarium Co-Op recommends a 20 gal long (76 L) and a group of 5-6; Seriously Fish specifies a 90x30 cm base (about 81 L) and a group of 8-10. We list 76 L, a 90 cm length, and a group of 8. Temperature: Seriously Fish gives 18-25 C, Aquarium Co-Op 18-24 C - both notably cooler than the 24-28 C many retail tags print.
description: The zebrafish is a species of danionin belonging to the genus Danio in the suborder Cyprinoidei. Native to South Asia, it is a popular, hardy aquarium fish, frequently sold under the trade name zebra danio.
native_range: South Asia, it is a popular, hardy aquarium fish, frequently sold under the trade name zeb

care_notes: Neons are soft-water fish that prefer the cooler end of tropical - Seriously Fish gives 21-25 C, which is meaningfully below the 26-28 C most community tanks run at, and long-term overheating is a common cause of short neon lifespans. Buy 8-10 at once; smaller groups hide and colour down. They should never be the first fish in a brand-new tank, as farmed stock is prone to neon tetra disease and to crashing in immature water. Dense planting and dim light bring out the colour.
common_mistakes: Adding them to an uncycled or newly set-up tank
Keeping them at 27-28 C long term, which shortens lifespan
Buying 4-6 instead of 8+, so they never school properly
Housing them with angelfish or other fish large enough to eat them as adults
Assuming losses in the first two weeks are normal rather than a sign of poor stock or an immature tank
disputed: Temperature is the key disagreement: Seriously Fish gives 21-25 C, while many retail and hobby sources give 22-28 C. We list 21-26 C and flag that sustained temperatures above 26 C are associated with shortened lifespan. Minimum volume commonly cited between 38 L and 54 L; Seriously Fish's 60x30 cm base (about 54 L) is the figure we use.
description: The neon tetra is a species of freshwater fish belonging to the family Acestrorhamphidae, the American characins, of the order Characiformes. The type species of its genus, it is native to blackwater and clearwater streams in the Amazon basin of South America. Its bright colouring makes the fish visible to conspecifics in the dark blackwater streams, and is also the main reason for its popularity among freshwater fish hobbyists, with neon tetras being one of the most widely kept tropical fish in the world.
native_range: blackwater and clearwater streams in the Amazon basin of South America

care_notes: Cardinals are larger, longer-lived and warmer-water than neons - 23-29 C rather than 21-25 C - so the two are not interchangeable despite looking similar. Much of the stock is still wild-caught from the Rio Negro and arrives stressed, so they need a mature, stable, soft, well-planted tank rather than a new setup. Buy 8-10 minimum. They are micropredators: crushed flake alone is not enough, and they do much better with daphnia, cyclops and baby brine shrimp.
common_mistakes: Treating them as identical to neons and keeping them too cool
Adding wild-caught fish to a tank less than a few months old
Buying small groups, which stresses them and dulls their colour
Keeping them in hard, alkaline water long term
Housing them with angelfish, which eat them once grown
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 54 L and 76 L. Aquarium Co-Op recommends 15-20 gal (57-76 L) for a school of 8-10; Seriously Fish specifies a 60x30 cm base (about 54 L). Difficulty is also disputed: Aquarium Co-Op presents them as a beginner schooling fish, while Seriously Fish's soft-water and mature-tank requirements put them above neons in difficulty. We list intermediate.
description: The cardinal tetra is a species of freshwater fish of the family Acestrorhamphidae, the American characins, of order Characiformes. It is native to the upper Orinoco and Negro Rivers in South America. Growing to about 3 cm (1.2 in) in total length, the cardinal tetra has the striking iridescent blue line characteristic of the genus Paracheirodon laterally bisecting the fish, with the body below this line being vivid red in color, hence the name "cardinal tetra". The cardinal tetra's appearance is similar to that of the closely related neon tetra, with which it is often confused; the neon's red coloration extends only about halfway to the nose, and the neon's blue stripe is a less vibrant blue.
native_range: the upper Orinoco and Negro Rivers in South America

care_notes: One of the few genuinely good nano schooling fish - fully grown at 2 cm, so a 45x30 cm tank works for a group of 8-10. They need gentle flow, dim light and dense planting, and their mouths are tiny, so crushed flake, nano pellets and baby brine shrimp rather than standard community food. Colour is dramatically better over a dark substrate in a planted tank. Soft, slightly acidic water suits them best but they adapt to moderately hard water.
common_mistakes: Feeding food too large for their mouths, so they slowly starve in a community tank
Strong filter flow, which exhausts them
Keeping 3-5 instead of 8+
Bare bright tanks, where they stay pale and hide
Housing them with anything big enough to swallow a 2 cm fish
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 19 L and 40 L. Aquarium Co-Op allows a small school in 5 gal (19 L); Seriously Fish specifies a 45x30 cm base (about 38-40 L). We list 38 L.
description: The ember tetra is a species of freshwater ray-finned fish belonging to the family Acestrorhamphidae, the American characins. This fish is found in the Araguaia River basin of Brazil. It was discovered in 1987 and named in honor of the fish explorer Heiko Bleher's mother, Amanda Bleher.
native_range: the Araguaia River basin of Brazil

images.attribution: (c) William Harmon, some rights reserved (CC BY)

care_notes: An excellent, genuinely hardy first schooling fish that tolerates a wide temperature and pH range but shows its best colour in soft, slightly acidic, well-planted water. Keep 8-10; in smaller groups they are nervous and stay near cover. Unusually for a rasbora they spawn by gluing eggs to the underside of broad leaves rather than scattering. They are peaceful enough for almost any community tank of similar-sized fish.
common_mistakes: Buying 5-6 rather than 8-10, so they never settle
Bright, bare tanks with no plant cover
Confusing them with the smaller lambchop rasbora (T. espei) and mixing the two groups
Housing them with fish large enough to eat a 5 cm fish
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 38 L and 54 L. Aquarium Co-Op allows a school of six in 10 gal (38 L); Seriously Fish specifies a 60x30 cm base (about 54 L) and a group of 8-10. We list 54 L.
description: The harlequin rasbora is a small fish in the family Cyprinidae. The species became an instant favorite among aquarists after its introduction in the early 1900s and is the best known and most widely kept species among the rasboras. In 1935, an image of a trio of harlequin rasboras, stamped in 14k gold, graced the cover of the first edition of William T. Innes's classic Exotic Aquarium Fishes, and remained through all 19 editions.
native_range: the fish's native waters, though this is not absolutely necessary if the basic water chemi

images.attribution: (c) Ashley Aucoin, some rights reserved (CC BY-NC)

care_notes: The exception among barbs: cherry barbs are genuinely peaceful and safe with long-finned fish, unlike tiger barbs. Males colour up deep red when kept in groups of 6-10 with several females present, and stay washed-out when kept singly or in pairs. They accept a wide pH and hardness range but want dense planting and shade. Endangered in the wild in Sri Lanka, so buy captive-bred stock.
common_mistakes: Assuming all barbs are nippy and excluding them from peaceful communities
Keeping 2-3 fish, so males never develop colour
Buying only males, which then spar constantly
Bright open tanks with no cover
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 38 L and 54 L. Aquarium Co-Op allows a school of six in 10 gal (38 L); Seriously Fish requires a 60x30 cm base (about 54 L) and 6-10 fish. We list 54 L.
description: The cherry barb is a tropical freshwater fish belonging to the family Cyprinidae. It is endemic to Sri Lanka, and introduced populations have become established in Mexico and Colombia. The cherry barb was named Puntius titteya by Paules Edward Pieris Deraniyagala in 1929. Synonyms include Barbus titteya and Capoeta titteya. It is the only species in the genus Rohanella.

care_notes: Tiger barbs are hardy and long-lived but genuinely nippy, and the nipping is worst in small groups and short tanks. A group of 8-12 in a tank of at least 80 cm redirects the aggression within the group; a group of four in a 60 cm tank will shred every long-finned tank mate. Never keep them with bettas, angelfish, guppies or any trailing-finned fish. They are boisterous eaters that outcompete slow, shy species at feeding time.
common_mistakes: Keeping fewer than 8, which turns aggression outward onto tank mates
Housing them with bettas, angelfish, guppies or fancy goldfish
Buying a small group for a 60 L tank
Assuming the aggression is a myth because juveniles in the shop look calm
Adding them to a tank of timid, slow feeders
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 72 L and 110 L. Seriously Fish specifies an 80x30 cm base (about 72 L); Aquarium Co-Op recommends 29 gal (110 L) and a group of at least seven, preferably 12+. We list the larger figure because group size is the main control on aggression. Temperature: Seriously Fish 20-26 C, Aquarium Co-Op 20-28 C.
description: The tiger barb or Sumatra barb, is a species of tropical cyprinid fish.
native_range: the southern portion of the eastern slope of Sumatra in Indonesia, where it is recorded fr

care_notes: Native across Pakistan, India, Nepal and Bangladesh, and a subtropical fish, not a tropical one: Seriously Fish gives 16-24 C. This is the single most important fact about them and the one most often got wrong - kept at 27-29 C in an unheated Indian tank in summer they are chronically stressed and short-lived. They also get large, to 7.5-10 cm, and need a 100 cm tank and a group of 8-10. Peaceful for a barb, but boisterous enough to bother very small or long-finned fish.
common_mistakes: Keeping them at tropical community temperatures instead of 16-24 C
Buying them for a 60 L tank based on 3 cm juveniles
Small groups, which makes them nippy
Housing them with slow long-finned fish
Assuming the long-finned ornamental strains have the same swimming ability as wild-type
disputed: Adult size is disputed: Seriously Fish says most are fully grown at 6.5-7.5 cm but some forms reach 9-10 cm; Aquarium Co-Op gives 7-10 cm. We list 10 cm. Minimum volume: Seriously Fish requires a 100x30 cm base (about 105 L), Aquarium Co-Op 29 gal (110 L) - these agree. Temperature is where the hobby is most often wrong; we follow Seriously Fish's 16-24 C.
description: The rosy barb is a subtropical freshwater cyprinid fish found in southern Asia from Afghanistan to Bangladesh.
native_range: southern Asia from Afghanistan to Bangladesh

care_notes: Angelfish are cichlids, not community centrepieces: they reach 15 cm long and up to 20 cm tall, so tank HEIGHT matters as much as footprint - aim for at least 45-50 cm of water depth or the fins deform. They eat anything that fits in their mouths, which includes neon tetras, ember tetras and shrimp once grown. Buy six juveniles and let a pair form, then be ready to rehome the rest, because a bonded pair will claim the whole tank when spawning. Warm water, 26-29 C, suits them best.
common_mistakes: Keeping them in tanks under 45 cm tall, which stunts and deforms the fins
Adding neon tetras or shrimp and being surprised when they disappear
Buying two 'to get a pair' and ending up with two fish that fight
Underestimating adult size from a 3 cm juvenile
Housing them with fin-nippers such as tiger barbs, which shred their trailing fins
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 110 L and 200 L. Aquarium Co-Op says 29 gal (110 L) supports up to four adults in a community tank and 55 gal (208 L) for a growing group of 5-6; Seriously Fish says 100x40x50 cm (about 200 L) should be the smallest considered. We list 200 L. Note that both agree height is a hard requirement, which volume alone does not capture.
description: Pterophyllum scalare, most commonly referred to as angelfish or freshwater angelfish, is the most common species of Pterophyllum kept in captivity. It is native to the Amazon Basin in Peru, Colombia, and Brazil. Particularly to the Ucayali river in Peru, the Oyapock River in French Guiana, the Essequibo River in Guyana, the Solimões, the Amapá, and the Amazon rivers in Brazil. It is found in swamps or flooded grounds where vegetation is dense and the water is either clear or silty. Its native waters range from a neutral pH of 7.0 down to near 6.0, with a general water hardness (gH) range of 3 to 10 °dH, and water temperature ranging from 26 to 30 °C. This is the species of angelfish most frequently found in the aquarium trade. A similar P. scalare exists in the Rio Orinoco. They are of the same size and shape, the only difference being the stripes; the Orinoco P. scalare has thinner, but dual, stripes.
native_range: the Amazon Basin in Peru, Colombia, and Brazil

care_notes: The most peaceful of the large gouramis and far more robust than dwarf gouramis, reaching 12 cm. They are labyrinth breathers and need access to a warm, humid air layer at the surface, so keep the lid on and the water gap small. Males display to each other but rarely do damage if there is space and cover; Practical Fishkeeping suggests two males to four females in a 120 cm tank. They are timid rather than aggressive and get bullied by boisterous tank mates - avoid tiger barbs and other nippers.
common_mistakes: Buying them for a 60 L community tank - they reach 12 cm
Keeping the tank in a cold room with a draughty open top, chilling the labyrinth organ
Housing them with fin-nippers, which target their long pelvic filaments
Keeping multiple males in a short tank with no line-of-sight breaks
Confusing them with the smaller and more disease-prone dwarf gourami
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 81 L and 200 L. Seriously Fish specifies 90x30x30 cm (about 81 L); Practical Fishkeeping recommends a 120 cm tank for a proper group of 2 males and 4 females. We list 110 L with a 100 cm footprint as a middle-conservative figure, and flag that a full group needs 120 cm.
description: The pearl gourami is a species of gourami native to Southeast Asia.
native_range: Southeast Asia

images.attribution: (c) Oskar King, some rights reserved (CC BY-NC)

care_notes: Dwarf gouramis are native to the Indian subcontinent and are sold everywhere as a beginner centrepiece fish, but farmed stock carries Dwarf Gourami Iridovirus (DGIV) at high rates - Seriously Fish cites research finding as many as 22% of Singapore-exported fish infected. DGIV is untreatable, usually fatal, and can pass to other species in the same water, so quarantine new fish. Almost all shop fish are male and males are territorial with each other, so keep one per tank unless it is very large. Keep them in a quiet tank with floating plants and gentle flow; they sulk and hide with boisterous tank mates.
common_mistakes: Buying two or three males for one tank, which leads to sustained bullying
Not quarantining, and introducing DGIV to an established community
Assuming a fish that stops eating and develops sores has a treatable bacterial infection
Keeping them in strong filter flow
Choosing them over the hardier honey gourami for a first centrepiece fish
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 38 L and 56 L. Aquarium Co-Op says 10 gal (38 L); Seriously Fish says a 60x30x30 cm (56 L) tank is 'just about big enough for a pair'. We list 56 L. Difficulty is genuinely disputed: Aquarium Co-Op rates them beginner-friendly and reports never seeing DGIV in its own stock, while Seriously Fish treats farmed stock quality as a serious problem. We list intermediate because the disease risk is a stock-quality lottery a beginner cannot assess.
description: The dwarf gourami is a species of gourami native to South Asia.

images.attribution: No machine-readable author provided. Fred Hsu assumed (based on copyright claims).

care_notes: Also native to India and Bangladesh, and the better choice over the dwarf gourami for almost every beginner: smaller at 5.5 cm, longer-lived, far less prone to iridovirus, and genuinely peaceful. Not a schooling fish, but they do better in groups of 4-6 where a loose hierarchy forms. They are slow, deliberate feeders and get outcompeted by fast fish such as danios and barbs. Floating plants and dim light bring out the honey colour and reduce shyness.
common_mistakes: Confusing them with the larger, dyed or hybrid 'sunset thick-lipped gourami' sold under the same name
Housing them with fast, greedy feeders that leave them nothing
Keeping them in bright bare tanks with no floating cover, so they stay hidden
Assuming a fish that hides is sick rather than intimidated
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 19 L and 76 L. Aquarium Co-Op says a single fish can live in 5-10 gal (19-38 L) and a group of three does better in 20 gal (76 L); Seriously Fish specifies a 60x30 cm base (about 54 L) for a pair or small group. We list 54 L for a pair and note 76 L for a group of three or more.
description: The honey gourami is a species of gourami native to India and Bangladesh.
native_range: India and Bangladesh

care_notes: Footprint matters far more than volume here: corys forage across the substrate all day, so an 80x30 cm base beats a tall 76 L cube. Use fine sand or smooth rounded gravel - sharp or dirty gravel erodes the barbels they feed with, and a barbel-less cory cannot find food. Keep six or more of the SAME species; mixed-species 'cory groups' do not shoal together properly. They must be fed directly with sinking food; they are not cleaners and will not survive on leftovers. They gulp air at the surface occasionally, which is normal.
common_mistakes: Sharp or unclean gravel, causing barbel erosion
Keeping two or three as a 'clean-up crew' instead of a group of six
Assuming they eat algae or leftovers and never feeding them sinking food
Mixing several cory species and counting them as one group
Keeping them at 28 C+ long term, which shortens lifespan
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 54 L and 76 L. Seriously Fish specifies an 80x30 cm base (about 72 L) for long-term care; Aquarium Co-Op recommends 20 gal (76 L). Group size: Seriously Fish says 4-6, Aquarium Co-Op says 6+. We list 6.
description: The bronze corydoras, also known as the green corydoras, bronze catfish, lightspot corydoras or wavy catfish, is a species of freshwater fish in the armored catfish family, Callichthyidae, often kept as an aquarium fish. It is widely distributed in South America on the eastern side of the Andes, from Colombia and Trinidad to the Río de la Plata basin; however, as presently defined it is a species complex and a taxonomic review is necessary. It was originally described as Hoplosoma aeneum by Theodore Gill in 1858 and has historically also been referred to as Corydoras aeneus.

care_notes: Kuhlis are burrowers and need soft sand or very smooth fine gravel; on coarse or sharp substrate they cannot bury themselves, stay stressed and can be injured. Keep at least six - kept alone or in pairs they hide permanently and owners assume they died. Feed sinking food after lights-out, since they are largely nocturnal and get outcompeted during the day. They squeeze through any gap, so cover filter intakes and every hole in the lid.
common_mistakes: Keeping one to three, so they never come out and are presumed dead
Coarse or sharp gravel that prevents burrowing
Not feeding them directly, on the assumption they scavenge enough
Uncovered filter intakes and open lid gaps, which they escape into and through
Adding them to a new, unstable tank - they are sensitive to nitrite and to copper-based medications
disputed: Species identity is genuinely unsettled: most fish sold as 'kuhli loach' in the trade are Pangio semicincta or P. oblonga rather than true P. kuhlii, and Seriously Fish has no P. kuhlii profile. Care is effectively identical across the group. Minimum volume commonly cited between 54 L and 76 L: Seriously Fish specifies a 60x30 cm base for P. oblonga; Aquarium Co-Op recommends 20 gal (76 L) for a group of three to six. We list 76 L. Temperature: Seriously Fish 21-26 C, Aquarium Co-Op 23-27 C.
description: The true Kuhli loach, which can be used synonymously with "coolie" loach, occasionally referred to as eel loach, is a small eel-like freshwater fish belonging to the loach family (Cobitidae). They originate from the island of Java in Indonesia. This serpentine, worm-shaped creature is very slender and nocturnal. Its distinctive orange-pink coloration with triangular black stripes and long lifespan makes it a popular aquarium species.
native_range: Indonesia Java, where collection of ornamental fish is extremely rare

images.attribution: (c) Lucas A. Giovannini, some rights reserved (CC BY-NC)

care_notes: This is the pleco to buy instead of a common pleco: it tops out around 10-13 cm rather than 50 cm. It needs real driftwood to rasp on for digestion, plus vegetables and sinking wafers - it will not survive on tank algae alone. Males are territorial with other males and with similarly shaped catfish, so keep one per tank unless it is large with several caves. They breed readily in caves, with the male guarding the eggs, so expect fry in an established tank.
common_mistakes: Buying it as an 'algae eater' and never feeding it, leading to slow starvation
No driftwood in the tank
Keeping two males in one tank
Confusing it in the shop with a juvenile common pleco, which looks similar at 5 cm
Assuming it will keep the glass clean once it is adult - adults eat far more prepared food than algae
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 54 L and 110 L. Seriously Fish says a 60x30 cm base (about 54 L) suffices for a single fish or breeding pair; Aquarium Co-Op recommends 20-29 gal (76-110 L). We list 76 L. Adult size: Seriously Fish 10-12.5 cm, Aquarium Co-Op 10-15 cm.
resolution_notes: cleaned 'Ancistrus cf. cirrhosus' -> 'Ancistrus' (non-binomial pattern: \bcf\.)
description: Ancistrus is a genus of nocturnal freshwater fish in the family Loricariidae of order Siluriformes, native to freshwater habitats in South America and Panama. Fish of this genus are common in the aquarium trade where they are known as bushynose or bristlenose catfish. In the aquarium hobby they are often referred to as bushynose or bristlenose plecos instead, but this may lead to confusion as "pleco" usually is used for Hypostomus plecostomus and its allies and is often used as a catchall term for any loricariids remotely resembling that species.
native_range: freshwater habitats in South America and Panama

care_notes: Do not buy this fish for a home aquarium. It is sold at 5 cm as a 'cleaner fish' and reaches over 50 cm, lives 10-20 years, and produces an enormous waste load. Aquarium Co-Op recommends starting at 75 gal (284 L) and moving up to 180 or even 500 gal (680-1900 L); Practical Fishkeeping says tanks of many hundreds of litres are required and criticises its sale for tanks as small as 40 L. Adults are nearly impossible to rehome and must never be released into local waterways, where they are highly invasive. Buy a bristlenose pleco or an otocinclus instead.
common_mistakes: Buying it as an algae eater for a 40-100 L community tank
Believing the myth that a fish grows only to the size of its tank
Not feeding it, so it rasps the slime coat off flat-bodied fish such as goldfish, angelfish and discus at night
Releasing an outgrown fish into a lake or river
Confusing it with a bristlenose pleco at point of sale
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 284 L and 1900 L. Aquarium Co-Op names 75 gal (284 L) as a starting point for a growing fish and 180-500 gal (680-1900 L) for an adult; Practical Fishkeeping declines to give a figure and says 'many hundreds of litres'. We list 680 L as the adult requirement and treat 284 L as juvenile-only. Scientific name is also unsettled - fish sold as 'common pleco' are variously Pterygoplichthys pardalis, P. multiradiatus or Hypostomus plecostomus, and are rarely identified at point of sale.
description: Pterygoplichthys pardalis, the Amazon sailfin catfish, is a freshwater tropical fish in the armored catfish family (Loricariidae). It is one of a number of species commonly referred to as the common pleco or "leopard pleco" by aquarists.
native_range: the Amazon River Basin of Brazil and Peru, preferring pH ranges of 7

care_notes: Otos are sold as an easy beginner algae eater but they are the opposite: most are wild-caught, arrive already starving after weeks in transit, and need to graze almost constantly. Only add them to a mature, planted tank at least a few months old that has visible biofilm and soft green algae. Supplement with algae wafers, blanched courgette and cucumber from day one rather than waiting to see if they run out of food. Keep six or more, and expect early losses from imported stock - a group that survives its first two months usually lives for years.
common_mistakes: Adding them to a brand-new tank with no established algae or biofilm
Assuming they will eat the brown or green algae you dislike and nothing else is needed
Buying one or two rather than a group of six
Buying visibly thin fish with sunken bellies
Using copper-based medications, which they tolerate poorly
disputed: Group size is disputed. Seriously Fish recommends at least six; Aquarium Co-Op argues against large groups on the basis that too many otos strip the tank of algae and then starve, preferring a couple of well-fed fish to a starving school. We list 6 and flag that a group is only appropriate in a tank with enough grazing to support it. Minimum volume: Seriously Fish specifies a 45x30 cm base (about 40 L); we list 54 L because the practical constraint is the amount of mature grazing surface, not swimming room. Difficulty: widely sold as beginner; we list intermediate.
description: Otocinclus macrospilus, the tailspotted oto, dwarf otocinclus or dwarf sucker, is a species of freshwater ray-finned fish in the armored catfish family Loricariidae. It is native to South America, where it is found in the upper Amazon basin in Colombia, Ecuador and Peru.
native_range: South America, where it is found in the upper Amazon basin in Colombia, Ecuador and Peru

images.attribution: (c) Kaden Slone, some rights reserved (CC BY)

care_notes: The standard wild-type-coloured form of the species and the most robust of the three colour strains, though still a genuinely demanding fish. Rams need hot water — Seriously Fish gives 27-30 C and Aquarium Co-Op calls 29-30 C the single most important husbandry factor; kept at the 24-25 C of a normal community tank they slowly decline and die, which is the most common cause of ram deaths. They also need soft, acidic, pristine water and a mature tank; they are poor competitors and should not go in a busy community. Warm Indian ambient temperatures actually suit this species well.
common_mistakes: Keeping them at standard community temperatures of 24-25 C
Adding them to a tank less than a few months old
Buying a pair from a tank of unsexed juveniles and getting two males
Keeping them in hard alkaline water
Housing them with fast, greedy feeders that outcompete them
Adding dwarf shrimp, which rams hunt
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 54 L and 76 L for a pair. Seriously Fish says a 60x30 cm base (about 54 L) is sufficient for one pair; Aquarium Co-Op recommends 20 gal (76 L) for a pair in a community. We list 76 L. Difficulty is disputed: Aquarium Co-Op rates them moderate, Seriously Fish's requirements (pristine water, 27-30 C, soft acidic, mature tank, poor competitor) put them at advanced. We list advanced.
description: The german blue ram is a selectively bred/wild-type colour form of Mikrogeophagus ramirezi, a dwarf cichlid native to the Orinoco River basin savannahs of Venezuela and Colombia.
native_range: the Orinoco River basin, in the savannahs of Venezuela and Colombia in South America (wild-type colouring; ornamental colour strains are captive-bred)

care_notes: A selectively bred gold/xanthic colour strain of the same species as the German Blue Ram, needing identical care: genuinely hot water (27-30 C — the single most important husbandry factor per Aquarium Co-Op), soft acidic pristine water, and a mature, uncrowded tank. Farmed gold-strain stock is often more inbred and hormone-treated than wild-type/German Blue stock, and tends to be noticeably less hardy with a shorter lifespan — buy from a breeder who can speak to the line's health where possible, not just the colour.
common_mistakes: Keeping them at standard community temperatures of 24-25 C
Adding them to a tank less than a few months old
Buying a pair from a tank of unsexed juveniles and getting two males
Keeping them in hard alkaline water
Housing them with fast, greedy feeders that outcompete them
Adding dwarf shrimp, which rams hunt
Assuming the gold colour strain is as hardy as wild-type/German Blue stock — it usually isn't

care_notes: A selectively bred, all-blue colour strain of the same species as the German Blue Ram, needing identical care: genuinely hot water (27-30 C — the single most important husbandry factor per Aquarium Co-Op), soft acidic pristine water, and a mature, uncrowded tank. Farmed electric-blue stock is often hormone-treated and more inbred than wild-type/German Blue stock, and is widely reported as the least hardy of the common colour strains — expect a shorter lifespan and source from a specialist breeder where possible.

care_notes: Keep exactly one. Rainbow sharks are solitary and become steadily more territorial as they mature, and both Seriously Fish and Practical Fishkeeping specify a 120 cm minimum tank for a single fish. They are most aggressive toward other bottom-dwelling grazers and toward anything with a similar shape - other rainbow sharks, red-tail sharks, plecos, loaches and corydoras. Provide caves and broken lines of sight. Juveniles hide constantly and look harmless in the shop, which is why they are so often bought for tanks that cannot contain an adult.
common_mistakes: Keeping two or more, which nearly always ends in one fish being killed
Buying one for a 60-100 L community tank based on juvenile behaviour
Housing them with corydoras, loaches, otos or plecos
Assuming they are an algae-eating utility fish rather than a territorial centrepiece
No caves or sight breaks, so the whole tank becomes one territory
disputed: Seriously Fish specifies a 120x45 cm base for a single specimen (about 240 L); Practical Fishkeeping gives 120 cm minimum, keep singly. Many retail guides say 55 gal (208 L) or even 30 gal (110 L). We list 240 L. Both trusted sources agree on the 120 cm length and on keeping them alone.
resolution_notes: GBIF says 'Epalzeorhynchos frenatus', iNaturalist says 'Epalzeorhynchos frenatum'
description: The rainbow shark is a species of Southeast Asian freshwater fish from the family Cyprinidae. It is also known as the ruby shark, red-fin shark, red-finned shark, rainbow sharkminnow, green fringelip labeo, whitefin shark and whitetail sharkminnow. It is a popular, semi-aggressive aquarium fish. Unlike true sharks, which belong to the Chondrichthyes lineage, the rainbow shark is an actinopterygiian.
native_range: the basins of Mekong, Chao Phraya, Xe Bangfai and Maeklong in Indochina

care_notes: The best algae eater in the hobby for hair algae and black beard algae, and large enough at 5 cm to survive most community fish. They cannot be bred in freshwater - the larvae need brackish or salt water - so every amano in the trade is wild-caught or specialist-raised, and they should be treated as long-lived pets rather than disposable clean-up crew. They need adequate GH and calcium to moult successfully; failed moults are the usual cause of unexplained deaths. Copper-based medications and many plant fertiliser overdoses are lethal to all shrimp. They climb out of open tanks, so use a lid.
common_mistakes: Copper-based fish medications, which kill shrimp at doses safe for fish
Soft, mineral-poor water causing failed moults
Assuming they will eat all algae including green spot algae, which they will not
Keeping them with fish that eat them - large cichlids, goldfish, big barbs
Open-topped tanks - amanos are determined escapers
Overfeeding the fish, after which the shrimp ignore algae entirely
disputed: Neither trusted source states a minimum tank size; Aquarium Co-Op describes them as suitable for 'nano tanks or larger'. We list 20 L as a practical floor because water stability, not swimming room, is the limiting factor. Adult size cited as 4-5 cm across Aquarium Co-Op's two guides. Temperature cited as 18-28 C and 18-27 C.
description: Caridina multidentata is a species of shrimp in the family Atyidae. It is native to Japan and Taiwan. Its common names include Yamato shrimp, Japanese shrimp, Amano shrimp, and algae shrimp.
native_range: Japan and Taiwan

care_notes: Start with at least 10 so you get both sexes, and expect a colony rather than individuals - they breed continuously in stable, mineral-rich water. They need GH of at least 6 degrees (110 ppm) and KH of at least 2 for successful moulting; soft water is the most common cause of colony collapse. Copper is fatal even at doses used to treat fish, so never medicate a shrimp tank with copper-based products. They live only 1-2 years, so a healthy colony replaces itself; a colony that stops producing young is telling you something about the water. Almost any fish will eat the babies.
common_mistakes: Copper-based medications and some plant fertilisers
Soft or RO water without remineralising for shrimp
Large water changes with mismatched temperature or TDS, which trigger fatal moults
Adding them to a new tank with no biofilm for the babies to graze
Expecting a visible population in a tank with fish that eat shrimplets
Keeping different Neocaridina colours together, which reverts the colony to wild brown in a few generations
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 15 L and 38 L. Practical Fishkeeping gives 15 L as an absolute floor; Aquarium Co-Op recommends a 10 gal (38 L) for a breeding colony. We list 20 L, because for shrimp the risk is water instability rather than crowding, and note that 38 L is a better target for a productive colony. Temperature: both agree on an 18-28 C tolerance with 21-26 C optimal. 'Livebearer' here means direct development - eggs hatch into miniature shrimp with no larval stage.
description: Neocaridina davidi, also known as the cherry shrimp, is a freshwater shrimp native to Taiwan, east of China, the Korean Peninsula, and Vietnam, that is sold globally in the aquatic pet trade. They are omnivores, and their natural habitat in these regions include inland water bodies such as lakes, ponds, rivers, and streams. N. davidi is also able to tolerate a wide range of environmental conditions, and as a result of this is also becoming invasive in thermally polluted waterways of Japan, the United States, Poland, and Germany. It is thought that the release of captive shrimp has led to their presence in these environments. Their natural coloration, or wild type, is a mottled brown, but N. davidi has been selectively bred to produce a diverse array of color morphs including red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet, white, clear, and more. The popularity of the red morph has led to N. davidi also being known as "cherry shrimp". N. davidi do not have a distinct larval stage, reach maturity in 30 days, and may live 1–2 years. At maturity, the shrimp are approximately 3–4 cm in length.

care_notes: The best algae-eating snail for a freshwater tank: they graze the algal film rather than plants, and will not eat healthy plants. They need hard, alkaline water with real calcium - in soft or acidic water the shell erodes and pits, which is irreversible. Practical Fishkeeping's rule of roughly one snail per 20 L keeps them fed; overstock them and they starve in a tank that looks clean to you. They lay hard white egg capsules on glass, wood and equipment that will not hatch in freshwater but are stubborn to remove. They climb out of open tanks and die on the floor.
common_mistakes: Soft or acidic water, which erodes and eventually breaches the shell
Buying six or more for a small clean tank, so they slowly starve
No lid, so they climb out and dry up
Copper-based medications and salt treatments
Assuming the white egg capsules are a disease or pest
Leaving an upside-down snail on the substrate - they often cannot right themselves
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 8 L and 20 L. Aquarium Co-Op says a nano tank of 2-3 gal (8-11 L) is enough; Practical Fishkeeping's stocking guidance of roughly 20 L per snail implies a larger tank if the snail is to feed itself. We list 20 L. Species identity is loose - 'nerite snail' covers several Neritina and Vittina species sold by shell pattern rather than by name.
description: Vittina natalensis, commonly known as spotted nerite, red spotted snail or zebra nerite, is a species of small freshwater snail with an operculum, an aquatic gastropod mollusk in the family Neritidae, the nerites. It returns to brackish waters to reproduce. This is a popular aquarium snail, sold because it looks attractive and eats algae in freshwater tanks, but can only reproduce in saltwater or brackish water conditions.

images.attribution: (c) Marco Vicariotto, some rights reserved (CC BY-NC-ND)

care_notes: Mystery snails are pets rather than a clean-up crew - they eat fish food, biofilm, dead plants and dead fish, but will not keep a tank clean. They reach 5 cm and need pH above about 7.2 and GH above 8 degrees (150 ppm) plus calcium-rich food, or the shell grows thin and pitted. Leave a 5-8 cm air gap under a tight lid: they lay pink egg clutches above the waterline and will climb out entirely if there is no gap or no lid. Cooler water extends their short 1-2 year life. Remove them before any copper or salt treatment.
common_mistakes: Soft or acidic water, giving eroded, thin shells
Filling the tank to the rim with no air gap, which they need to breathe and lay eggs
No lid, so they escape and dry out
Copper-based medications and aquarium salt
Housing them with puffers, loaches or assassin snails, which eat them
Assuming a snail sealed in its shell for a day or two is dead
disputed: Naming and taxonomy are genuinely muddled: Aquarium Co-Op lists both Pomacea diffusa and P. bridgesii, and most trade 'mystery snails' are P. diffusa sold under the P. bridgesii name. This matters legally, since some Pomacea species are restricted or banned as invasive in several countries - check local regulations before listing this species by region. Minimum volume: Aquarium Co-Op says 5 gal (19 L); we list 20 L.
description: Pomacea bridgesii, common name the gold Inca snail, spike-topped apple snail or mystery snail, is a South American species of freshwater snail with gills and an operculum, an aquatic gastropod mollusk in the family Ampullariidae. These snails were most probably introduced to the United States through the aquarium trade.

care_notes: A hardy, adaptable tetra that fades from black to grey with age — a normal colour change, not a health problem. Can nip fins, especially in too-small a group, so keep 6 or more to spread out any nippiness and avoid pairing with long-finned, slow fish like bettas or fancy guppies.

care_notes: A tightly-schooling tetra known for its bright red nose and precise, synchronised swimming in a large enough group — genuinely more sensitive to water quality than beginner tetras like neons, and its schooling behaviour and nose colour are both a reliable indicator of good/poor water. description: Hemigrammus erythrozonus, the glowlight tetra, is a species of freshwater ray-finned fish belonging to the family Acestrorhamphidae, the American characins. This fish is found in the Essequibo River and the Courantyne River in Guyana and Suriname. It is silver in colour and a bright iridescent orange to red stripe extends from the snout to the base of its tail, the front of the dorsal fin being the same color as the stripe. Other fins are silver to transparent. The glowlight tetra is a peaceful, shoaling fish. It is larger than the neon tetra, and its peaceful disposition makes it an ideal, and popular, community tank fish. It should be kept with similar sized, non-aggressive species. Hemigrammus gracilis is a senior synonym. The red-line rasbora of Malaysia and Indonesia has markings and coloring very similar to H. erythrozonus, but is a member of order Cypriniformes, not a close relative.

description: The White Cloud Mountain minnow is a hardy species of freshwater fish and coldwater fish often kept in an aquarium. The species was considered to be a member of the carp family of the order Cypriniformes, although now it is placed in the family Tanichthyidae. This species is native to China. The White Cloud Mountain minnow is practically extinct in its native habitat, due to pollution and tourism. It was believed to be extinct for over 20 years in 1980, but an apparently native population of this fish was discovered on Hainan Island, well away from the White Cloud Mountain. They are bred in farms and are easily available through the aquarium trade. However, inbreeding in farms has led to genetically weak stock that is vulnerable to disease and prone to physical deformities.

description: The walking catfish is a species of freshwater airbreathing catfish native to Southeast Asia. It is named for its ability to "walk" and wiggle across dry land, to find food or suitable environments. While it does not truly walk as most bipeds or quadrupeds do, it can use its pectoral fins to keep it upright as it makes a wiggling motion with snakelike movements to traverse land. This fish normally lives in slow-moving and often stagnant waters in ponds, swamps, streams, and rivers, as well as in flooded rice paddies, or temporary pools that may dry up. When this happens, its "walking" skill allows the fish to move to other aquatic environments. Considerable taxonomic confusion surrounds this species, and it has frequently been confused with other close relatives. One main distinction between the walking catfish and the native North American ictalurid catfish with which it is sometimes confused, is that the walking catfish lacks an adipose fin. It can survive 18 hours out of water.
native_range: Southeast Asia

description: Cichla ocellaris, sometimes known as the butterfly peacock bass, is a very large species of cichlid from South America, and a prized game fish. It reaches 74 cm (29 in) in length. It is native to the Marowijne and Essequibo drainages in the Guianas, and the Branco River in Brazil. It has also been introduced to regions outside its natural range, but some uncertainty exists over the exact identity, and at least some of the introductions may involve another Cichla species or hybrids. description: Neolamprologus multifasciatus are one of the small shell-dwelling cichlids endemic to Lake Tanganyika in east Africa. The male reaches 5 cm (2 in) in length, and the female only 2.5 cm (1 in) in the aquarium. In the wild, they reach only 3 centimetres (1.2 in) in standard length of male and female reaches less than 2.2 centimetres (0.87 in) in standard length. This makes them one of the smallest species within the Cichlidae family. Adults are often a light brown to beige and exhibit a characteristic dark vertical banding pattern with a bright white or blue iris and black pupil. The body is fusiform and slightly laterally compressed. Caudal fins are rounded with a single light band across the peripheral. Anal fins are also rounded and solitary, lacking a second fin. Unlike other species of African cichlids which have egg spots on the caudal fin to distract predators, N. multifasciatus lay eggs within the protected interior of gastropod shells and subsequently lack egg spots. Pectoral fins are rounded and transparent while the pelvic fins are wing shaped with a white leading edge. The rear edge of both the dorsal and anal fins are drawn-out. The lateral line is straight but discontinuous. The jaw is superior (upturned) with the lower jaw extending more anterior than the upper jaw. Only one nostril can be found on each side of the head, instead of the two nostrils found in most other fish.

description: Nimbochromis venustus, commonly called venustus hap or giraffe hap, is a Haplochromine cichlid endemic to Lake Malawi in Africa. It prefers the deeper regions of the lake where it hunts smaller juvenile cichlids with a specialised hunting technique. After spotting prey, it will partially submerge itself into the sand and lie motionless until the chosen fish comes within reach. It will then dart out of the sand and strike. It is related to Nimbochromis livingstonii. In the wild it is known to grow to 25 centimetres (9.8 in) TL though usually not exceeding a length of 22.5 centimetres (8.9 in) TL.

description:
The fork-tailed paradisefish, or paradise gourami, is a species of pelagic, long-finned freshwater ray-finned fish in the family Osphronemidae, found in most freshwaters of East Asia ranging from eastern China down to northern Vietnam. This anabantiform fish can reach a standard length of 6.7 cm, though most are only about 5.5 cm .
Paradise fish were the second Chinese ornamental fish introduced to the West after the Goldfish, and the first freshwater tropical fish successfully bred in captivity in Europe, having been imported 1869 to France by the French aquarium fish importer Pierre Carbonnier in Paris. The paradise fish is one of the more aggressive members of its family. It is more aggressive than the three spot gourami, yet less pugnacious in nature than the less commonly kept combtail.
native_range: most freshwaters of East Asia ranging from eastern China down to northern Vietnam

description: The licorice gourami is a species of freshwater ray-finned fish from the subfamily Macropodusinae, part of the family Osphronemidae, the gouramis. It is endemic to Bangka in Indonesia where it is found in the slow, flowing streams with black waters associated with peat swamp forests. This species was formally described by the Dutch ichthyologist Pieter Bleeker as Osphromenus deissneri in 1859 with the type locality given as Sungai Baturussa basin at 8 kilometres from Pudingbesar on the road to Kampong Simpan, Bangka. It is the type species of the genus Parosphromenus. The specific name honours F. H. Deissner, a military health officer, who sent a collection of specimens of fishes from Bangka to Bleeker which included the type of this species.

description: Badis badis, also known as the blue perch or blue badis, is a small species of Asian freshwater fish in the family Badidae of the order Anabantiformes. It is found in ponds, rivers, ditches and swamps in northern India, eastern Pakistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan and Nepal, including the Ganges, Brahmaputra, Mahanadi and Indus basins. It is sometimes kept as an aquarium fish. It is a small, predatory fish that feeds on tiny invertebrates. Maximum total length is around 8 cm (3 in). It is sexually dimorphic, with males growing larger and more colorful, especially when excited, compared to females. Adult males have blue fins and may display dark vertical bands on the flanks, while the smaller females display little color. Several similar relatives, now recognized as separate Badis species, have historically been confused with Badis badis. Historically the two genera that now make up the Badidae, Badis and Dario, were placed in the family Nandidae; this is no longer the case.

description: The Japanese rice fish, also known as the medaka, is a member of genus Oryzias (ricefish), the only genus in the subfamily Oryziinae. This small native of Japan is a denizen of rice paddies, marshes, ponds, slow-moving streams and tide pools. It is euryhaline, occurring in both brackish and freshwater. It became popular as an aquarium fish because of its hardiness and pleasant coloration: its coloration varies from creamy-white to yellowish in the wild to white, creamy-yellow, or orange in aquarium-bred individuals. Bright yellow, red or green transgenic populations, similar to GloFish, have also been developed, but are banned from sale in the EU. The medaka has been a popular pet since the 17th century in Japan. After fertilization, the female carries her eggs attached anterior to the anal fin for a period before depositing them on plants or similar things.

description: Gymnarchus niloticus – the aba, aba aba or frankfish – is an electric fish, living at the bottoms of rivers and lakes. It is the only species in the genus Gymnarchus and the family Gymnarchidae, within the order Osteoglossiformes. It is a long slender fish with no pelvic or anal fins, and a tail fin shaped like a rat's tail. It swims using its elongated dorsal fin, allowing it to keep its body straight while it moves. This in turn enables it to produce a steady but weak electric field, which it uses to locate its prey. It is large for a river fish; adults can reach 1.6 m (5.2 ft) in length and 19 kg (42 lb) in weight.

These factors have influenced the species' popularity in captivity, and it is commonly kept by aquarists and other hobbyists.

description: Polypterus endlicheri, the saddled bichir, is one of the fourteen extant species in the Polypteridae family. Polypterus comes from the Greek words poly and pteron, roughly translating to "many finned", while endlicheri is derived from the Austrian botanist Stephen Endlicher, who first identified the fish from a collection at the Naturhistorisches Museum in Vienna. The common name, saddled bichir, comes from the saddle-like patterns that line the dorsal side of the fish. P. endlicheri has also earned nicknames such as "dragonfin" or the "dinosaur bichir" because of its prehistoric appearance.

description: The alligator gar is a euryhaline ray-finned fish in the clade Ginglymodi of the infraclass Holostei, being most closely related to the bowfins. It is the largest species in the gar family (Lepisosteidae), and is among the largest freshwater fishes in North America. The fossil record traces its group's existence back to the Early Cretaceous over 100 million years ago. Gars are often referred to as "primitive fishes" or "living fossils", because they have retained some morphological characteristics of their early ancestors, such as a spiral valve intestine, which is also common to the digestive system of sharks, and the ability to breathe in both air and water. Their common name was derived from their resemblance to the American alligator, particularly their broad snouts and long, sharp teeth. It is suggested that an alligator gar can grow up to 10 ft (3.0 m) in length.
native_range: North America

description: Channa gachua, the dwarf snakehead, is a species of fish in the family Channidae. The name "dwarf snakehead" is also used for several other species of small snakeheads. C. gachua is native to freshwater habitats in southern Asia, where it has a wide distribution from Iran to Indonesia. This fish is considered to be a species complex, a group of several closely related taxa with one name. A few species such as Channa harcourtbutleri have been separated from the complex in recent decades. The easternmost population of C. gachua is often recognized as a separate species C. limbata, while the isolated Sri Lankan population often is recognized as C. kelaartii.

description: Channa is a genus of predatory fish in the family Channidae, commonly known as snakeheads, native to freshwater habitats in Asia. This genus contains about 50 scientifically described species. The genus has a wide natural distribution extending from Iraq in the west, to Indonesia and China in the east, and parts of Siberia in the Far East. A particularly high richness of species exists in Myanmar (Burma), Bangladesh and northeastern India, and many Channa species live nowhere else. In contrast, a few widespread species have been introduced to several regions outside their natural range, where they often become invasive. The large and medium-sized Channa species are among the most common staple food fish in several Asian countries, and they are extensively cultured. Apart from their importance as a food fish, snakeheads are consumed in some regions as a traditional medicine for wound healing and reducing postoperative pain and discomfort, and collected for the international aquarium pet trade.
native_range: freshwater habitats in Asia

description: The hogchoker is a small species of flatfish found along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of North and South America, ranging from Massachusetts to Venezuela. They prefer brackish water, and the nominate subspecies is abundant in many bays and estuaries north of the Carolinas. It is a member of the American sole family Achiridae. They are usually brown to dark brown in color, and lighter on their "blind side". The overall body color is often broken by a series of spots and thin stripes, which can be lighter or darker than the main body color. The fins and tail have fringed edges helping hide the fish from its prey. They mainly feed on small aquatic insects and invertebrates. They get their common name because East Coast fishermen would feed these so-called "trash" fish to their hogs, after which the fish would bow its body into a suction cup and stick to the soft palate of the hog, rather like peanut butter in a dog's mouth.

description: Leptochilus pteropus is a species of aquatic or semi-aquatic fern, commonly known as Java fern. It is predominantly known from Malaysia, Thailand, Northeastern India and parts of South China. It is a highly variable plant, with several different geographic varieties and physical forms that vary in leaf size, texture and shape. Found in its natural habitat growing attached to riparian roots and rocks, it can grow fully or partially submerged, provided its roots and rhizome remain wet. The plant will readily propagate asexually by producing small, adventitious plantlets from the leaf tips and margins of established, mature foliage. The small sprouts quickly develop roots of their own, and, if water currents facilitate it, may attach themselves to surrounding objects before the "mother" leaf expires. In the event that the mother leaf wilts or detaches prior to the plantlet establishing itself, the small fern will float on its own to a new location to start anew.

description: Limnophila aromatica, the rice paddy herb, is a tropical flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae. It is called ngò ôm, ngò om, or ngổ in Vietnam and used as an herb and also cultivated for use as an aquarium plant. The plant was introduced to North America in the 1970s due to Vietnamese immigration following the Vietnam War. It is called "ma om" in Khmer. It is used in traditional Cambodian soup dishes and Southern Vietnamese cuisine. It can grow in flooded rice paddies during wet season but it grows best on drained but still wet sandy soil of harvested rice paddies for a few months after the rainy season ended. It dies out soon after it flowers. Rural Cambodians often harvest them and put them on the roof of their houses to dry for later use.

description: Pistia is a genus of aquatic plants in the arum family, Araceae. It is the sole genus in the tribe Pistieae which reflects its systematic isolation within the family. Its native distribution is uncertain but is probably pantropical; it was first scientifically described from plants found on the Nile near Lake Victoria in Africa. It is now present, either naturally or through human introduction, in nearly all tropical and subtropical fresh waterways and is considered an invasive species as well as a mosquito breeding habitat. The specific epithet is derived from a Greek word, στρατιώτης, meaning "soldier", which references the sword-shaped leaves of some plants in the genus Stratiotes.

description: Crinum thaianum, also called the Thai onion plant or water onion, or Phlap Phueng Than, is an emergent plant species, endemic to the coastal plain of Ranong and Phang Nga Provinces, Thailand. These growth habits make it a popular addition for tropical aquaria, and it is sold in many regions to be used specifically for growth within displays of tropical fish. In nature, however, the species is threatened with extinction, and diminishing rapidly, due to habitat destruction.

description: Semaprochilodus insignis, the kissing prochilodus or flag-tailed prochilodus, is a species of freshwater ray-finned fish belonging to the family Prochilodontidae, the bocachicos or flannel-mouth characiformes. It is native to central and western parts of the Amazon basin. It is migratory, moving in large groups into whitewater rivers to spawn, afterwards returning to blackwater and clearwater rivers, as well as flooded forests. It is important in fisheries and sometimes seen in the aquarium trade, but requires a relatively large tank. It can reach a maximum standard length of 27.5 cm (10.8 in) and weight of 560 g (1.23 lb). It generally resembles the other members of the genus Semaprochilodus, but this species possesses yellow fins as opposed to the red in the other species except for S. kneri, which it closely resembles, differing only in some traits of meristics and osteology. Adult S. insignis lack the dark flank spots that can be seen in adult S. taeniurus, but both species have these spots as juveniles.
native_range: central and western parts of the Amazon basin

description: Nannostomus unifasciatus, commonly known as the one-lined pencilfish, is a freshwater species of fish belonging to the genus Nannostomus in the characin family Lebiasinidae. They are popular in the aquarium trade due to their small size, beautiful color pattern, unique swimming posture and relative hardiness. With its long, pencil-shaped profile, its single jet black stripe reminiscent of the graphite core of a pencil, and its eraser-colored caudal fin, this is the species for which the popular name, 'pencilfish', was first coined in the 1920s, later to be applied to all the species of the genus Nannostomus.

description: The European bitterling is a temperate freshwater ray-finned fish belonging to the family Acheilognathidae, the bitterlings. It originates in Europe, ranging from the Rhone River basin in France to the Neva River in Russia. It was originally described as Cyprinus amarus by Marcus Elieser Bloch in 1782, and has been referred to in scientific literature as Rhodeus sericeus amarus. It is known simply as "the bitterling" in its native range, where it is the only species of its genus Rhodeus, and sometimes in the scientific literature, also, but this is technically wrong, being a leftover from the times when the European bitterling was united with its Siberian relative, the Amur bitterling, in R. sericeus. Properly, "bitterling" can refer to any species of Acheilognathus or Rhodeus.

description: Poecilia velifera, known as the Yucatán molly or giant sailfin molly, is a poeciliid fish native to the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico. It is typically under 10 cm (3.9 in) in length, but may reach 15 cm (5.9 in), with males somewhat larger than females. It belongs to a group of mollies known as sailfins, named for the large males' sail-like dorsal fin, a feature that is especially pronounced in P. velifera. The species occurs in a range of habitats, from coastal lagoons, estuaries, and salt marshes to freshwater pools in the interior of the peninsula; it is particularly associated with mangrove swamps and sinkholes known as cenotes.
native_range: the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico

description: The swordtail platyfish is a species of ray-finned fish in the family Poeciliidae. The species is endemic to the Soto La Marina River basin in Tamaulipas and Nuevo León. It lives in springs, streams, arroyos, ditches, marshes, and ponds in slow-flowing clear to muddy waters, often over mud, clay, gravel, and rock where vegetation is typically abundant. Males grow 3 cm (1.2 in) in length whereas females grow to 4 cm (1.6 in) in length, however both sexes can reach 1 cm (0.4 in) over their usual length. Gestation is usually 24 to 35 days, where around 20 to 50 young are born.

description: The redtail splitfin or redtail goodeid is a species of goodeid fish from the family Goodeidae and subfamily Goodeinae. Like other members of Goodeinae, the redtail splitfin is native to Mexico and a livebearer. However, the goodeid mating system differs in several ways from the more common livebearing fish from the family Poeciliidae that includes guppies and swordtails. While no goodeid species is a very popular aquarium fish, the redtail splitfin is one of the most popular. Only the male has the red-orange tail for which it is named. Its specific name honours the collector of the type, Gustav Eisen (1847–1940) who was Curator of Marine Invertebrates at the California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco, California.

description: Fundulopanchax scheeli, the emerald aphyosemion, is a species of killifish, endemic to the lower Cross River basin in Nigeria. It is a coastal rainforest fish which lives in small streams and ponds. It prefers a temperature of around 75 °F (24 °C), and a slightly acidic pH around 6–7. The specific name honours the Danish count, army colonel, explorer and ichthyologist Jørgen J. Scheel (1916–1989). F. scheeli grows to a maximum size of 6 centimetres (2.4 in) total length. It is considered to be critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature due to its very small area of occupancy and faces threats from herbicides and pesticides used in agriculture, such as in rice farming, and from deforestation.

description: The striped panchax is a species of killifish, of the genus Aplocheilus. An aquarium variant of this species with a more yellowish coloration is known as golden wonder killifish. The striped panchax inhabits fresh and brackish waters of India and Sri Lanka. It is found in streams, rivers, swamps, and paddy fields. In the wild it feeds on insects, crustaceans, and even small fishes. It grows to a length of 10 cm (4 in). Most male A. lineatus measure around 7 centimetres (3 in), but the fish can grow up to 10 centimetres (4 in) under excellent conditions, especially if brought to the end of its life expectancy, around six years. It possesses a parietal eye which permits it to see prey insects and predators above it on the surface. A. lineatus can jump very well.

description: The blue panchax or whitespot is a common freshwater fish found in a large variety of habitats due to its high adaptability. This species is native to southern Asia from Pakistan, India, Malaysia to Indonesia. It has been discovered in two hot springs in Singapore. The species also commonly spotted in Johor Bahru rivers and estuaries. Identified by a white-coloured spot on its head, the species can reach up to 9 cm (3.5 in) in length; it tends to keep to the surface of the water, and controls the mosquito population by feeding on their larvae.

description: Pachypanchax playfairii, the golden panchax, is a species of Aplocheilid killifish, the only species of freshwater fish endemic to the Seychelles, a group of islands in the Indian Ocean, east of Tanzania. It is the only member of its genus found outside of Madagascar. Within the Seychelles it is found only on the granitic islands. Here it occurs in small freshwater and brackish water streams, feeding on worms, crustaceans, insects and fish. An egg scatterer, the golden panchax breeds amongst floating water plants. This species is unusual in that the scales of the male become lifted during the breeding season, giving the skin a rough appearance. Unlike the true annual killifish, they live as long as similar fishes, a few years, 3 years is not uncommon 5 is unknown.

description: The golden topminnow is a fish of the genus Fundulus and is a United States native fish mostly distributed throughout the southeast, ranging from Kentucky and Ohio south into Florida. Although it has such a wide distribution throughout the south, the habitats and micro-habitats that it occupies do not differ much from one area of distribution to others. The golden topminnow is a small surface feeding fish that tends to reproduce late in the spring season and on into the early parts of the summer, and although the fry reach maturity fairly quickly the longevity of the golden topminnow is quite short. Because the golden topminnow is lower in the trophic level and is a small fish, it primarily feeds on small and/or drifting organisms at, or near the surface of, vegetated areas. This particular topminnow is not currently listed as an endangered species, nor does it have any particular type of management plan.

description: Herotilapia multispinosa also known as the rainbow cichlid is a Central American freshwater fish of the cichlid family. It is found on the Atlantic slope of Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica from Patuca River (Honduras) south to Matina River, and on the Pacific slope of Nicaragua and Costa Rica from Guasaule River south to Tempisque River. Specimens are also reported from the Choluteca River on the Pacific side of Honduras. This species is found in lakes and swamps with muddy bottoms, where it uses its specialized teeth and only 3.5% jaw protrusion to feed mostly on algae. It is commercially important as an aquarium fish. The rainbow cichlid prefers a pH range of 7.0–8.0, water hardness of 9-20 dGH and a temperature range of 21–36 °C.

description: The Burmese Border loach, angelicus loach or polka dot loach, Botia kubotai, is a recently described species that has quickly become a popular tropical fish for freshwater aquariums. description: Pseudosphromenus dayi or Indian spiketail betta is a species of freshwater ray finned fish from the subfamily Macropodusinae, part of the gourami family Osphronemidae. It occurs in Kerala on both the coastal regions and the Western Ghats. It is a species of still or slow flowing waters, especially lakes, ditches and swamps in both fresh and brackish waters. Pseudosphromenus dayi is a bubble nester, the male creates a nest made of bubbles under an overhang or a leaf. The females lays eggs which drop to the substrate and are picked up by both fishes in the pair and placed in the bubble nest. The name Polyacanthus cupanus dayi was first published in 1908 by Köhler in 1908 but Catalog of Fishes refers to this as a nomen nudum and attributes the valid use of the name, with a formal description, to P. Engmann in 1909. The type locality is given as Malacca which is probably an error and should be Kerala. The specific name honors the British ichthyologist and author of the Fishes of India, Francis Day (1830–1889).
